title: Hunga Tonga: the sky rang like a bell

link.method: pooled Pearson r over the gauges with a barometer: hourly max |air pressure jump| vs the same gauge's hourly max |water residual|, water lagged 0..6 h

lanes.method: lanes: largest barometer jump vs mean gauge envelope

arrivals.method: Pearson r across gauges: time the barometer jump first exceeds 5 x its pre-eruption sd vs time the water residual first does

stats.largest water oscillation: Port San Luis 1.284 m at 13.25 h after the eruption

gaps: Air push = real barometers at the tide gauges (NOAA CO-OPS, every 6 minutes): the jump is the pressure minus its own 3 hour running mean, shown as the hourly largest |jump|; gauges without a barometer show no pillar.
The air push lane shows the largest jump among the stations each hour, so each passing of the wave over any station is a spike; between passings it shows ordinary weather wiggles.
ERA5 (a model, hourly at about 31 km) smooths the same wave to a few tenths of hPa; it is kept in the data only as a check.
The ring is a reference front drawn at 315 m/s from the USGS origin, not data.
Gauge series = hourly maximum of |water level minus tide prediction minus a 3 hour running mean|, from 6 minute data: it keeps the amplitude of the oscillation, not its sign.
Ocean tsunami waves travel slower than the air wave; at far gauges the water responds first to the air wave (meteotsunami), then to the ocean tsunami hours later.
The ERA5 point is the 0.25 deg grid cell nearest each gauge.

The arrival link (r across gauges) is high partly because both the air wave and the water response arrive later at farther gauges; the hour by hour pooled link is weak because the water keeps ringing for many hours after a one hour air pulse.
Key West and San Juan (Atlantic side) show no clear ERA5 pressure peak; their water response comes about a day later.

hero_norm.method: largest barometer jump among the stations, before the eruption (no other baseline year makes sense for one eruption)
